Biggest story: yesterday's broad relief rally is being tested before the open by a sharp front-end sell-off. In the prior session the S&P 500 rose 2.346256% to 7549.94, the Nasdaq Composite rose 2.740992% to 25253.14, the Dow rose 2.152685% and the Russell 2000 led with +3.148282%. This morning ES is -0.594118229527676%, NQ is -1.0896143068767958% and Dow futures are -0.11809973713284316%. The US 2Y is up 11.94bp to 4.6809% and the 10Y is up 6.82bp to 4.9502%, while Bund (-0.7bp) and Gilt (+0.9bp) barely moved, so this is a US-specific, front-end-led bear flattener. The cause has not been verified in our news searches. Oil is down about 3% (WTI 84.33, Brent 89.49) and gold is down 1.9358% to 4059.68. The VIX closed at 21.0 vs 19.92 even as stocks rallied, which says hedging demand did not fade. Credit contagion check: the computed HY contagion read shows the Caa–B gap at 772bp, against a 5-year average of 419.04bp, at the 99.2156862745098th 5-year percentile. It is +203bp over 3 months and +62bp over 1 month, but -8bp on the week, and it is the widest since 2020-04-16. Caa OAS is 1083bp (97.6470588235294th 5-year percentile). So far the rot has not visibly climbed the ladder. Single-B is 311bp (+18bp in 1m, ~50th 5-year percentile), Ba is 197bp (+12bp in 1m, ~51st percentile), the B–Ba gap is 114bp (41st percentile) and IG is 89bp (43rd percentile). The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes has risen from 0.346 three months ago to 0.662, back near its 5-year median of 0.692. Co-movement is normalising, but the spread is not leaking into single-B levels. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. AI backstop: CoreWeave 5Y CDS is 1221.7bp, 27.2bp above the 1,194.5bp Oct 15 record. That is 103.7% of the run from the 452bp June low. It tightened 48.3bp in the latest session but is +68.2bp on the week. Nvidia's own 5Y CDS is 140.69bp, down 2.87bp on the day and 4.96bp on the week. The CDS market is therefore keeping the stress on the neoclouds rather than on the guarantor, so it is not yet pricing the backstop as a liability. Nvidia's equity tells a less comforting story: it is -11.58% on the week and its DRSK model-implied CDS (30.9) sits at the 100th 1-year percentile. This is descriptive only. Tech phase model: the basket is in Phase 1 ('initial drop, credit calm'), 24 days past its peak, with a -17.56% drawdown vs -13.29% for the 2000 basket at the same point. Three signposts have triggered: CoreWeave CDS through its record, breadth (71.43% of basket names more than 20% off their highs vs a 50% line) and SOX at -31.44% from its 52-week high vs -30%. The phase model's 6-month Phase 2+3 odds fell 8.1pp vs Nov 6, and its 12-month 'ever Phase 2+' odds fell 4.7pp. Rally conditions (VIX spike-and-turn with calm credit) are on, but the model's history has a 44.1% trap rate. Sentiment: a defensive tape that is willing to bounce. The bounce now needs the rates move and CoreWeave credit to stop deteriorating.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Computed MA stats (no active crosses on any asset): S&P 500 is 7549.94, 1.64% below its 50DMA (7676.211) and 3.03% above its 200DMA (7328.2249), at the 98th percentile (z 2.68). The index is caught between its two trend lines: the short-term trend is broken, the long-term trend is intact. Historically, the computed reversal frequency is 44% after death crosses and 33% after golden crosses (n=9 each). That is the base-rate probability of a trend change after a cross, and it is low enough that a cross, if one comes, has more often been followed through. Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 50th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +79bp.

Latest reading is +0.77 vol points (57th percentile of the 65 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.53 (50th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), improving over the past 3 months (-0.08 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.50pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +79bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 1bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 86.0 (59th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 74bp (flatter by 14bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

⚠ Commentary is 40 days old (as of 2026-10-01); it may not reflect the latest Fed news.

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 58/100 — Sticky but not re-accelerating. The underlying-trend gauges cluster tightly around 2.3–2.8%: Median CPI 2.61% (falling), 16% trimmed-mean CPI 2.66%, median PCE 2.67%, trimmed-mean PCE 2.26%, core sticky CPI 2.78%. Most read 'flat' and sit only modestly above their historical middle. The computed core-trend sub-score, shown separately, reflects that. The hot spot is the flexible basket (6.12%, rising, 82nd percentile), and the Dallas distribution is bimodal. 26.8% of the PCE basket is inflating above 5% (16.6% above 10%), but 25.6% is outright falling. Inflation pressure is concentrated in energy-sensitive, volatile items rather than spread through services. Falling crude helps. Core PCE at 3.12% and a 3.1% wage pace keep the Fed from declaring victory, but 1-year breakevens at 1.91% and 5-year at 2.27% show markets are not pricing a persistence problem (analyst estimate for the persistence score).

🫧Tech Bubble Peak Again?vs March 2000
BUBBLE RESEMBLANCE · SUPER COUNT computed
9 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 7 beyond 2000 — 59/100
Today is far from March-2000 equity froth but close to, or beyond, 2000 on easy credit and financial conditions. The tape now looks more like the early bust than the peak. Equity Froth is low on the computed indicators: Nasdaq trailing P/E 39.31x is 15% of the way to the 175x 2000 peak, Nasdaq stretch vs its 200DMA is 1%, and SOX P/E is at 36%. Late-cycle Catalyst is split. Credit tightness exceeds 2000 levels (IG 126%, Baa–10Y 156%) and the curve is at 71%, but PMIs show no rollover (1% and 13%). Macro Regime: commodities vs equities at 200% and the dollar at 40%. Bear-market signposts: loose financial conditions (NFCI 148%) and VIX complacency (132%) are past 2000 readings, while retail sentiment (AAII 14%), confidence (31%) and margin growth (40%) are not euphoric. The phase model places the tech basket in Phase 1 (initial drop, credit calm), 24 days past its peak, with a -17.56% drawdown that is deeper than 2000's -13.29% at the same point. Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

The 2000 analogy is about how the drawdown unfolds, not the valuation level. Today's Nasdaq multiple is a fraction of 2000's, but the leadership group is cracking the same way. Semis are 31.44% off their 52-week high, 71.43% of the basket is more than 20% off its highs, and the neocloud credit tail (CoreWeave CDS 1221.7bp, notes yielding about 15%) is where the stress first shows. In 2000 the bust became systemic only when credit widened. Today HY OAS is 326bp, 94–122bp short of the model's Phase 2 triggers, and the equity-regime model puts 89.2% on 'volatile bull' with credit 97.2% 'calm'. The rally-watch conditions are on (VIX spike-and-turn, calm credit, oversold). History says these bounces are traps 44.1% of the time (typical +10.3% over 13 days) and real otherwise (typical +31.3% over 86 days). The model's historical tilt at this phase mix favours gold, Treasury duration and IG over mega-cap growth, developed international and EM. Analyst-estimate inputs: S&P top-10 weight about 38% (37.8% reported at Aug 31), CAPE about 39 (40.5–41 reported mid-2026, before the drawdown), market cap/GDP about 228% (above 237% reported in September, since de-rated). IPO froth is about 55/100: megadeals such as SpaceX's $75bn and Anthropic's planned $75bn+ show frothy supply, but some issuers are postponing.

Odds the volatility-washout conditions line up within a week: 54%; within two weeks: 56%. Rallies of 8%+ that start in this phase: 44% later fail below their starting low (median 13 trading days, +10%); the rest become recoveries (median 86 days, +31%). Descriptive, not a signal.

Positioning tilt (generic, historical): Historically, at this phase mix the phase-conditional optimum has favoured gold, Treasury duration and investment-grade credit, over mega-cap growth, developed international and emerging markets.

Phases are rules with the same thresholds in 2000 and today: Phase 2 = HY OAS +150bp or Baa-10y +50bp from the basket's peak; Phase 3 = Sahm rule or ISM < 47 for 3 months AND bank stress (KBW -25% or C&I charge-offs >= 1% and rising); Phase 4 = basket +20% off its low, above its 200-day average, HY 150bp off its wide. Odds come from every Nasdaq-100 drop since 1985 that reached today's depth, weighted by how closely its credit, macro and volatility readings matched today's, plus a small labelled judgment overlay for AI-credit stress. 'Ever P2+' = chance spreads cross the Phase-2 line at any point before the horizon. Model estimates on ~40 episodes: read them to within +/-10 points. Not financial advice.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Inference: hold at the next (December) meeting with a hawkish tilt. Core PCE at 3.12%, unemployment at 4.1% and claims at 189k give little cover for a cut. At Jackson Hole, Warsh's argument implied the policy rate should, if anything, move higher (OMFIF). The 11.94bp jump in the 2Y this morning fits a hawkish repricing, but we have not verified a Warsh-specific catalyst.

~1 YEAR

Inference: a smaller Fed footprint, achieved gradually. He has argued since his April confirmation hearing for a smaller balance sheet coordinated with Treasury, with advance notice to Congress and markets (KSL/Kitco). Later readings suggest the balance sheet is 'not going anywhere fast', with unconventional tools 'used sparingly, if at all' (OMFIF). Rates are likely flat-to-higher over the year unless underlying inflation falls clearly below its current 2.6–2.8% trend. The view that a smaller balance sheet makes room for lower rates is his stated long-run rationale, not a near-term promise.

Warsh took over in June. The Fed held rates steady while he launched five task forces on communications, the balance sheet, the inflation framework, data and productivity (Semafor, Jun 17). His on-record themes are 'regime change' at the Fed, a preference for the policy rate over the balance sheet as the main tool (Newsquawk, Bloomberg Government), central-bank independence (FXStreet, Apr 21), and a smaller balance sheet over time (Fortune, Apr 21). We found no November 2026 Warsh speech, and the current fed funds range is n/a in this data. All forward calls above are inferred from his prior statements, not from new guidance.
